model.iron_lamination: TRANSVERSE-ISOTROPIC: the 2D materials' homogenised curve in the sheet plane, the insulation-limited series average across the stack (solver.axial_mu, k_f = 0.92 from the same material the 2D curve was laminated with).  Measured mu_r: stator 742 in plane / 12.3 axial, rotor 162 / 11.7.

two_d.solver: fem_solver_2d weak form (P2, full ring, static3d cross-section mirrored), CONVERGED Picard — ref2d.solve_2d_reference_converged
two_d.relaxation: geometric in log(mu), adaptive, constitutive-residual stop

shipped_relaxation.verdict: NOT a solution: its Picard limit-cycles at a constitutive residual of ~0.8 and breaks the machine's exact anti-periodicity by 3 %. Kept for the before/after only.

mesh_errors.3D_basis: three cross-sections at the saturated point, 1.46937 / 1.47227 / 1.46943 T (isotropic model, round 3), and two formulations 0.6 % apart on one mesh
mesh_errors.2D_basis: five cross-sections from 4 025 to 12 769 triangles with the converged relaxation: 1.52010 / 1.51951 / 1.51868 / 1.51528 / 1.51542 T (0.3 % total spread, the two finest 0.01 % apart)

demag.note: negative H.Mhat is demagnetising; at I=0 the END elements sit at a LESS negative H than the mid-plane ones because the end flux spills into air instead of being pushed back through the magnet
demag.measured_on: the ISOTROPIC iron (round 3) — the exposure SHIFT between the end and mid slices is a ratio inside the magnets, which the iron anisotropy moves far less than it moves the axial spill, but it has not been re-measured.

bracket.note: phi=0 forces B normal to the truncation surface, dphi/dn=0 forces it tangential; the true answer lies between, so the spread is a BOUND on the truncation error, not an estimate
bracket.measured_on: the ISOTROPIC iron at max_iter 45 (round 3) — not re-run for the laminated model.  It bounds the TRUNCATION error only (0.008 % on k_flux_self), and nothing about the air box changed, so it is carried over rather than re-spent; the lamination change it does NOT cover is quoted separately below and is 200x larger.

_schema._doc: 3D end-effect passport for ONE machine (magnet-only, I = 0).

fields.geometry_fingerprint: routes.simulation._geometry_fingerprint of the geometry this was solved for; a passport whose fingerprint does not match the active design describes a different motor and must be ignored.
fields.machine: slots/poles/radii/stack/materials actually solved, mm and T.
fields.model: sector angle, periodicity sign, element order, air box, mesh sizes, z levels — everything needed to reproduce.
fields.k_flux: axial mean of the gap fundamental over the stack, divided by the 2D fundamental. Multiply a 2D flux linkage / EMF / back-EMF constant by this.
fields.k_flux_self: same average divided by the 3D MID-PLANE value: the pure end effect, with any 2D-vs-3D modelling difference removed. k_flux = k_flux_self * (B1_3D_mid / B1_2D).
fields.spill_profile: z stations (m, and z/(L/2)) with B1(z) in T and B1(z)/B1(0). Stations beyond z/(L/2) = 1 are OUTSIDE the iron and are the fringing tail, not stack flux.
fields.two_d: the 2D reference: solver, mesh, B1 and the 3D-mid/2D ratio.
fields.demag: H.Mhat per axial magnet slice; negative is demagnetising.
fields.bracket: Dirichlet vs Neumann outer boundary at the chosen box — a CONSERVATIVE bound on the truncation error, not an estimate.
fields.solves: dofs, elements, wall time and Picard state of every solve.
fields.consistency_investigation: why the two_d check fails, measured — one block per round of investigation, each naming what was ruled out and how. Read this before trusting or re-deriving k_flux.

consistency_investigation._doc: Why the 3D-vs-2D check failed, measured, in four rounds: the magnet law (fixed, 40b7de7), the mu_r ladder (the cross-section mesh, not the formulation), the 8 % that survived rounds 1-3, and round 4 — the 2D solver's saturation state was never a solution, and the 3D iron was missing an anisotropy 2D cannot have.
consistency_investigation.status: RESOLVED — 3D mid-plane and 2D now agree to 0.80 % on the same cross-section (tolerance 2 %), k_flux is usable

round_1_magnet_law.finding: fem_solver_2d assembled M where the law B = mu0*mu_r*H + mu0*M demands M/mu_rec; 2D magnets were 5 % strong

round_2_the_mu_r_ladder.the_hypothesis: the residual grew with mu_r and vanished without iron, which is the signature of the TOTAL scalar potential cancelling inside high-mu iron (B = -mu grad phi, large times small)

test_a_exact_iron_benchmark.what: magnetised sphere inside a concentric iron shell, which has a CLOSED-FORM solution at every mu_r (static3d.exact.sphere_in_shell_B).  One mesh, 56680 tets; three formulations; mu_r = 1 .. 1e6.  Reproduce with: python -m motor_ai_sim.simulation.static3d.benchmarks --ladder
test_a_exact_iron_benchmark.conclusion: every error is FLAT in mu_r (spread x1.11 to x1.16 over mu_r = 10..1e6), and the total scalar potential at P2 is the MOST accurate of the three in the iron — about 2.7x better than the lowest order edge element on the same mesh.  The hypothesis had the two scalar potentials swapped: it is the REDUCED potential that cancels in iron, which is why the TOTAL potential is the standard cure for it.

test_b_the_residual_is_the_CROSS_SECTION.what: the machine itself, linear iron at mu_r = 4625, 3D scalar P2 sector vs the 2D solver on the SAME cross-section, refining the in-plane element size of the SOLID regions and nothing else
test_b_the_residual_is_the_CROSS_SECTION.conclusion: the residual converges MONOTONICALLY to zero with cross-section refinement — both legs converge onto B1 = 0.0576 T — so it is discretisation error, and it is in the thin rotor bridges.  The passport above was solved at h_solid = 1.2 mm, between the first two rungs.
test_b_the_residual_is_the_CROSS_SECTION.why_it_looks_like_a_mu_r_effect: with LINEAR iron at mu_r >~ 200 the un-saturated rotor bridges short ~96 % of the magnet flux, so the gap fundamental is the small remainder and is proportional to 1/mu_r (d ln B1 / d ln mu_r = -0.91 measured between mu_r = 1000 and 4625).  A sub-percent error in the bridge reluctance is then a several-percent error in B1.  The amplifier is the BRIDGE SHUNT, not the potential — and it is an artefact of running the iron linear: the real machine saturates those bridges (mu_r ~ 5) and B1 is 1.47 T, not 0.058 T.

test_c_it_is_not_an_end_effect.what: the same linear mu_r = 4625 case at 1x, 2x and 4x the stack, against the same 2D reference
test_c_it_is_not_an_end_effect.conclusion: flat — a finite-stack effect would close as the stack grows, and this does not

test_d_the_nedelec_formulation_does_not_.what: the same ladder solved in the A-formulation on Nedelec edge elements (static3d/nedelec.py), same mesh, same Region list, same post-processing
test_d_the_nedelec_formulation_does_not_.conclusion: the edge element's residual grows with mu_r too, in the OPPOSITE direction, and the three formulations straddle the 2D answer by 20 % at mu_r = 4625.  That is what a mesh-limited quantity looks like, and it settles the Stage-B question: the vector potential is not a fix for this, and on the same mesh the lowest-order edge element is the least accurate of the three.

round_3_what_is_left.the_number: with the magnet law fixed and both models converged, the NONLINEAR machine's 3D mid-plane gap fundamental sits about 8 % above the 2D solver's on the same cross-section: 3D 1.470 T +/- 0.2 %, 2D 1.36 T +/- 1 %
known_contributions: Picard noise: the 2D leg moves about 1 % between sweep counts on a fixed mesh (and 3.1 % on the passport's own cross-section, where 16 sweeps is an outlier at 1.328 T against a 1.355-1.369 T cluster); the 3D leg stops at its 45-sweep cap with a constitutive residual of 6.4e-3 against a 3e-3 tolerance. That is noise ON the residual, not the residual.

the two Picards do not agree on what |B| an element has: fem_solver_2d averages |B| over the quadrature points, static3d.solver takes |mean B|, and on a saturating bridge those are different points on the same curve. Note the SIGN before blaming it: the 2D convention reads the LARGER |B|, so it saturates the bridges more, shunts less and should read HIGHER — the opposite of what is measured. Reconciling it would widen the gap, not close it, which is exactly why it has to be reconciled before anything else is concluded.

cross-section resolution is NOT it at this operating point: refining h_solid from 1.5 to 0.6 mm moves the 3D leg by 0.2 % and leaves the ratio at 1.077 — the saturated bridges do not amplify a mesh error the way the linear ladder's un-saturated ones did
next_steps: make the two element-|B| definitions the same and re-measure — it is the one KNOWN difference in how the two models read the same B-H curve, and its sign says the true gap is wider than 8 %
converge both Picards (raise the 3D cap; give fem_solver_2d the adaptive geometric damping and constitutive-residual test static3d already uses) so the +/-1 % noise stops masking the next effect
then compare something that is NOT the gap fundamental — magnet flux and bridge flux at the mid-plane — to say WHERE the two models put the flux differently, which the gap harmonic alone cannot

nonlinear_vs_cross_section_resolution._doc: the SAME nonlinear machine at three cross-section resolutions, 3D scalar P2 sector vs the 2D solver on that same cross-section — the round-2 refinement test, repeated at the real (saturated) operating point
nonlinear_vs_cross_section_resolution.note: this does NOT converge the way the linear ladder did, and the reason is visible in the columns: the 3D leg is steady to 0.2 % across the three meshes (1.46937 / 1.47227 / 1.46943 T) while the 2D leg wanders by 1.8 % (1.36093 / 1.38567 / 1.36439 T) and the ratio wanders with it.  A saturated bridge does not amplify a mesh error the way an un-saturated one does, so at the REAL operating point the mesh is no longer the story: the 3D answer is converged, and what is left is a genuine ~7-8 % model disagreement with 1-3 % of 2D Picard limit-cycle noise on top

three_way_on_a_coarser_cross_section._doc: the same nonlinear machine solved three ways on ONE mesh (h_gap 0.45 mm, h_solid 1.5 mm, box 60.0 mm, 108675 tets) with the 2D leg on the same cross-section — the three-way the Nedelec spike was commissioned to produce

the_2d_leg_is_converged_too._doc: the 2D reference alone, on four cross-sections and at four Picard sweep counts each — because 'the other model is under-resolved' is the easiest thing to assume and the cheapest thing to check
the_2d_leg_is_converged_too.conclusion: 1.36 T +/- 1 %, with no trend in either direction — the 2D leg is mesh-converged and its Picard noise is about 1 %.  Both models are therefore converged, roughly 8 % apart, and that gap is a MODEL difference, not a numerical one.

superseded_blocks.linear_iron_3D_over_2D_by_mu_r: the ladder recorded here in the first pass (0.9151 at mu_r = 4625 up to 0.9451 at mu_r = 10) was taken with the pre-40b7de7 2D leg; multiplied by the 4.94 % magnet-law factor it becomes the -3.9 % to -0.8 % ladder the round-2 tests above explain and remove
superseded_blocks.linear_note: the original conclusion — 'the offset does not vanish as mu_r falls, so it is NOT the total scalar potential's cancellation' — was right about the cancellation and wrong about the reason: the offset at low mu_r was the magnet law, and the growth with mu_r was the bridge-shunt amplification of the mesh error

suspect_1_lamination_homogenisation_PRIM.hypothesis: the 3D iron eats the RAW steel curve while the 2D iron eats the k_f-homogenised one, so 3D iron is 1/0.92 more permeable and the iron-shunted magnet circuit lands the gap flux HIGHER

measurement.how: static3d.motor_geometry builds its regions from the SAME fem_solver_2d.build_materials call the 2D leg uses; the curves were compared point by point
measurement.note: the raw-vs-laminated gap is 0.15 T, so the null result is a measurement, not a tolerance artefact

suspect_2_bh_interpolation.verdict: FALSIFIED — there is only one implementation
suspect_2_bh_interpolation.measurement: both legs call field_ops._mu_r_from_bh_vec on the same curve object (H(B) linear in B, differential mu0 above the last sample); static3d.solver imports it from field_ops precisely so it cannot drift

suspect_3_the_magnets.measurement: the 2D magnets carry a 2nd-quadrant demag curve, but solve_magnetostatics_fem's Picard updates DOM_STATOR, DOM_ROTOR and DOM_SHAFT only — both models hold the magnets linear at mu_rec = 1.05

suspect_4_the_2d_picard_fixed_point_CAUS.verdict: CONFIRMED — the whole of the 8 %, and 4 % more
suspect_4_the_2d_picard_fixed_point_CAUS.what_is_wrong: fem_solver_2d relaxes the B-H fixed point arithmetically in nu with a fixed 0.5 damping and stops when the STEP is small.  On a saturating spoke rotor it limit-cycles: the state it returns violates the curve it was handed by ~80 %.

shipped_relaxation.why_the_harmonics_are_a_test: 7 poles per 180 deg sector makes the machine EXACTLY anti-periodic, so B_r(theta+pi) = -B_r(theta) and every EVEN harmonic of B_r is zero in any solution.  The nonlinear problem is monotone and has exactly one solution, so 3 % of even harmonic is 3 % of field that is not physics.

converged_relaxation.how: same weak form, same mesh, same materials, same curve — geometric damping in log(mu), adaptive step, stopped on the constitutive residual || |B|(nu_curve - nu_used) || / || |B| nu_curve ||
converged_relaxation.validated: bit-identical to solve_magnetostatics_fem at equal permeability (zero nonlinear sweeps), pinned by tests/test_static3d_stage_a.py::test_the_converged_2d_leg_is_the_shipped_weak_form
converged_relaxation.conclusion: 1.515-1.520 T across five cross-sections (0.3 % spread, the two finest 0.01 % apart), anti-periodicity restored to 0.03 %, and 11-12 % above the shipped relaxation on the same meshes

suspect_5_the_mu_field_transplant.verdict: INCONCLUSIVE BY CONSTRUCTION — recorded so it is not re-run
suspect_5_the_mu_field_transplant.why: it transplanted the 2D limit cycle's permeability, not a fixed point's (its two anti-periodic copies differ by 90 % in the mean).  The control failed too: quantising mu into 48 log bins (max 10 % error) moved the 2D gap fundamental by +32 % — which is its own result, the saturated bridge shunt is stiff enough that a few percent of mu is tens of percent of gap flux, and that is why a badly relaxed Picard lands so far out.

round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy._doc: A physics gap this comparison surfaced, not a tuning knob: across a stack, steel and insulation are in SERIES, so mu_z is insulation-limited at mu0/(1-k_f) = 12.5 mu0 against an in-plane 4600.  A 2D model cannot represent it at all; the 3D model was solving a solid block, which let end-region flux cross the laminations as if they were steel.

one_mesh_one_flag.cross_section: h_gap 0.35, h_solid 1.2, box 160 mm, P2, 90-sweep cap

round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy.RE_QUOTE: k_flux_self moves from 0.97503 to 0.95944, i.e. -1.6 %, which is 200x the truncation bracket (0.008 %) this passport quotes as its error bar.  The end-effect answer for the 40 mm is therefore materially different from every previous revision, and it is a physics correction, not a fit: blocking the axial path through the laminations makes MORE of the magnet flux reach the gap at the mid-plane (+2.5 %) and LESS of it survive toward the ends (-1.6 % on the axial mean).
round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy.and_it_closes_the_check: with solid iron the 3D mid-plane sits 3.24 % below the converged 2D leg; with the stack's own anisotropy, 0.80 % — inside the 2 % agreement tolerance, so k_flux is usable for the first time
round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy.pinned_by: tests/test_static3d_stage_a.py::test_axial_permeability_of_a_stack — asymptotics, monotonicity in k_f, and the k_f = 1 identity against the isotropic assembly, bit for bit

round_4_the_same_defect_in_the_productio._doc: The static field path and the torque path have their own loops.  Measured at the preset's stored operating point (43.84 A, 13000 rpm, gamma 10 deg), not assumed.

static_field_path.who: fem_field2d / solve_field2d_on_mesh -> solve_magnetostatics (P1); solve_magnetostatics_fem (P1/P2) is the same three lines
static_field_path.verdict: SAME DEFECT — not converged, 8-9 % low in the gap

no_load._doc: solve_magnetostatics (P1) and solve_magnetostatics_fem (P1/P2) on the mirrored full-ring cross-section at I = 0. The spoke rotor's bridges are already saturated with no current at all, which is why the no-load case is a real test. The LOADED case is in loaded_static.json (this mesh carries no coil regions, so the loaded rows produced here were duplicates and have been removed).

torque_path.verdict: CLEAN — it does not rely on the Picard
torque_path.how_it_solves: a pointwise NEWTON on the field residual to 1e-7, with the damped Picard only as a seed and a fallback.  A Newton-converged A satisfies K(nu(|B(A)|)) A = f, which IS the constitutive law, so its field residual bounds the constitutive residual.

round_4_the_same_defect_in_the_productio.proposed_fix: scratchpad/fem_solver_2d_picard.patch — geometric damping in log(nu), adaptive step, constitutive-residual stop, cap raised 8 -> 60, and a loud warning when the fixed point is not reached.  Verified on a patched COPY: 1.51952 T in 62 sweeps at residual 9.3e-4, against the shipped 1.38472 T on the same problem.  NOT committed — fem_solver_2d is change-controlled.

l_stack_curve_note: ISOTROPIC iron and the OLD (unconverged) 2D leg — every k_flux in these rows is stale by the two corrections in consistency_investigation round 4. k_flux_self is the isotropic model's; the laminated model moves it by -1.6 %.
